articles.title: Google Maps now shows the ‘Gulf of America’
articles.summary: Google Maps has renamed the “Gulf of Mexico” to “Gulf of America” for US users on mobile and desktop.
articles.body: Google Maps now shows the “Gulf of America” in place of the “Gulf of Mexico” for users on both web and mobile in the United States. It made the change after the Trump administration formally changed the name today of the body of water spanning between the eastern coast of Mexico and Florida. Google says it follows the GNIS, or Geographic Names Information System, a US database of location information. Users in Mexico will continue to see “Gulf of Mexico,” while the rest of the world will see the original name with “Gulf of America” in parentheses. Google says it determines a user’s location — and thus which version of the body of water they see — using data from their mobile OS, SIM, and network. Desktop users will see changes based on search settings or device location if not provided. [Image: Google Maps says “Gulf of America” and Apple Maps says “Gulf of Mexico.” Meanwhile, Apple hasn’t made any changes in Apple Maps yet, although it does redirect “Gulf of America” searches to the Gulf of Mexico. Other mapping companies like MapQuest have not made changes either. However, we found that Google-owned Waze shows both names if you search for “Gulf of Mexico,” but finds nothing when searching for “Gulf of America.”

articles.title: Apple Maps now shows the Gulf of America
articles.summary: Apple is renaming the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America on its Maps app.
articles.body: Apple is renaming the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America in its Maps app. The company started rolling out the name change for US users this afternoon, and Bloomberg reports that it will soon display the name for users globally, too. Google Maps started showing the “Gulf of America” for users in the US on Monday. President Donald Trump signed an executive order for the name change in January, and the change entered the federal naming database, the Geographic Names Information System, this week. Unlike Apple, Google Maps displays different names depending on a user’s location. Users in Mexico will continue to see the body of water labeled as the “Gulf of Mexico,” and users in other countries will see “Gulf of Mexico” alongside “Gulf of America” in parentheses. Other mapping apps, like Microsoft’s Bing and MapQuest, continue to show the Gulf of Mexico. Apple currently offers its Maps app across the iPhone, iPad, Mac, and in beta on the web. The Verge reached out to Apple with a request for more information about the change but didn’t immediately hear back.

articles.title: Four Fed bank boards wanted rate hike before July 2026 hold
articles.summary: Directors at the Cleveland, Minneapolis, Kansas City, and Dallas Fed banks backed a quarter-point increase before policymakers voted to hold
articles.body:
Directors at four Federal Reserve regional banks voted to increase the primary credit rate in the days before the Fed's July meeting, discount rate minutes released Tuesday showed, providing fresh evidence of how divided the central bank was heading into that decision.

The directors of the Cleveland and Minneapolis Fed banks voted on July 16, 2026, and the directors of the Kansas City and Dallas Fed banks voted on July 23, to set the primary credit rate at 4%, a quarter-percentage-point increase from the existing level of 3.75%. The Board of Governors took no action on those requests and approved maintaining the rate at 3.75%.

At the July 28–29 joint meeting of the Board and the Federal Open Market Committee, policymakers voted to keep the federal funds target range at 3.5% to 3.75%. Three FOMC members dissented, according to Reuters . Regional Fed bank directors have no role in setting the federal funds rate and hold no FOMC seats, but they convene regularly with their bank presidents and those presidents say the directors' perspectives inform their own policy thinking.

Notably, Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid lacked a voting seat on the FOMC this year, according to Reuters, so his bank's directors pushed for a rate hike at a meeting where he was unable to cast a dissenting vote himself.

At the July 20 Board meeting — held the week before the FOMC convened — directors at ten Reserve Banks had voted to keep the primary credit rate at its existing level. Only the Cleveland and Minneapolis boards had at that point voted for an increase, and the Board took no action on those requests then either.

The three officials who dissented at the July meeting in favor of a rate increase were Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari, and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan. All three argued the Fed needed to act to bring inflation back to its 2% target. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who sided with the majority, said the central bank had not abandoned its inflation goal but cautioned that elevated prices could not be resolved quickly.

The Board's vote to hold at the July 29 meeting was unanimous. Voting for the action were Chairman Kevin Warsh, Vice Chair Philip Jefferson, Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman, and Governors Christopher Waller, Lisa Cook, Michael Barr, and Jerome Powell.

images.caption: Four Fed bank boards wanted rate hike before July 2026 hold · Quartz · Smith Collection / Gado / Getty Images

articles.title: Ontario threatens electricity amid Trump-Canada trade war. What would that mean for US?
articles.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford is threatening to cut off Canadian power to the U.S. in retaliation for President Trump’s trade war, a move that could boost already high electricity prices in some states. On Monday, Ford told The Associated Press that “everything is on the table,” including cutting off electricity to the U.S. “We power 1.5 million…
articles.body:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford is threatening to cut off Canadian power to the U.S. in retaliation for President Trump’s trade war, a move that could boost already high electricity prices in some states.

On Monday, Ford told The Associated Press that “everything is on the table,” including cutting off electricity to the U.S.

“We power 1.5 million homes and businesses,” he said. “Everything’s on the table. I’ll do whatever it takes.”

He made similar remarks during a Wednesday press conference, calling on other regions of Canada to join him.

“Everything’s on the table, but I can’t do it alone,” Ford said. “I’m not the only province that ships electricity down to the U.S. We need a Team Canada approach.”

Any effort to cut off electricity to the U.S. would come on top of retaliatory tariffs already announced by Canada on $27.6 billion in U.S. goods, including steel, aluminum, fish and cheese.

That move came after the U.S. imposed a 50 percent tariff on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods.

If Ford or other Canadian ministers move forward with threats to cut off electricity, that could raise already rising prices Americans are paying for power.

In total, Canada supplied less than 1 percent of the total electricity used in the U.S. last year.

However, that’s not divided evenly among states, as some in the northern U.S. get a more significant share of their power from the neighboring country.

“If we don’t receive the imports from Canada, we have to switch on more expensive plants, and we could get the power from those more expensive plants, but we would be then increasing our CO2 emissions, in addition to paying higher costs,” said John Parsons, a senior lecturer at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Sloan School of Management and a researcher with its Center for Energy and Environmental Policy.

Parsons noted that this electricity could be more expensive because it runs on gas, which, unlike renewable power, would require the purchase of fuel.

In a follow-up email, he said that exact costs could be difficult to calculate but estimated that a shutoff of Canadian power could end up costing between $300 million and $600 million per year.

Doug Arent, global fellow at the Columbia University Center on Global Energy Policy, said that Ontario on its own would not likely make a material difference, saying if Ford cut off power to the U.S. unilaterally, it would be more of a “symbolic gesture.”

However, if more provinces were involved, Arent said, Americans in the Northeast U.S. could see prices rise if a shutoff lasts more than a few days.

“If it’s off for days or weeks, then in that month, there might be price impacts,” he said.

NYISO, the power grid operator for New York, a state that gets some power from Ontario, said it anticipates having enough electricity to meet its needs.

“The U.S. and Canada have one of the most integrated electric grids in the world, allowing system operators in both countries to pool resources for improved reliability and economic efficiency,” Kevin Lanahan, NYISO senior vice president of external affairs and corporate communications, said in a statement.

“We are in close and regular contact with Hydro Quebec and Ontario’s Independent Electricity System Operator. The NYISO anticipates having adequate supplies to meet expected demand on the system,” Lanahan said.

Mary Cate Colapietro, spokesperson for grid operator ISO New England, said in an email that it “would not anticipate reliability issues tied to reduced imports, at least under typical weather conditions.”

“In the event Canadian provinces reduce (or entirely cut) the amount of electricity they are sending to New England, we would expect the impact to largely be financial, in the form of higher wholesale market prices. We would also anticipate emissions in the region increasing. The potential for higher wholesale prices would be due to a change in the supply/demand balance,” Colapietro said.

She noted that her region is not connected to Ontario, where Ford has authority.

Meanwhile, Trevor Sutton, a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, said the uncertainty about how the situation will play out could make planning difficult.

“Both sides appear to be willing to use their tools but also withdraw them in a very fluid way. … And if you’re an electricity operator, planning around that is almost impossible,” Sutton said.

The potential increases come as Americans are already struggling with rising power prices as infrastructure upgrades and increasing demand drive up utility bills.

In July, U.S. electricity costs were 4.2 percent higher than they were the year before, outpacing general inflation, which sat at 3.4 percent year over year.

Parsons said that in his area, prices were increasing because of costs for new power infrastructure that transmits and distributes electricity. He noted that further south, data centers are also playing a role.

Canada’s action could be “a relatively small portion of the electric bill, but everybody is already up in arms about their electric bill, so everything that adds to it is a problem,” Parsons said.

images.caption: U.S. and Canadian flags are displayed before an event with Ontario Premier Doug Ford and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, Feb. 11, 2025, in Washington.

articles.title: Hackers steal data from millions of UK airport customers
articles.summary: About 8.7 million customers had their data accessed and a ransom was demanded.
articles.body:
Three major UK airports have been hit by a "cyber security incident" in which criminal hackers accessed the data of almost nine million people and demanded a ransom.

Manchester Airports Group (MAG), which owns Manchester, East Midlands and London Stansted airports, said customers' contact details, vehicle registrations and postcodes were obtained by hackers at the weekend.

MAG told the BBC the hackers demanded a ransom fee for the return of the data, which the group said it refused to pay. The sum of the ransom fee was not disclosed.

The firm said "at no point has passenger safety or aviation security been compromised" and the system hacked did not hold customers' bank or payment details.

The data of about 8.7 million customers was accessed.

The majority of the data accessed was restricted to customer email addresses and related to WiFi sign-ups within the airports' terminals, MAG said.

MAG said in a statement: "We would like to reassure customers that Manchester Airport Group takes the security of customer information extremely seriously and we apologise for any inconvenience or concern caused."

The firm said it only became aware of the hack on Tuesday and quickly prevented the hackers gaining any more access, and notified affected customers.

"We immediately contained the risk and have been working with specialist advisors and taking appropriate steps to protect our customers and systems," MAG said.

"We have informed and are working with the relevant authorities."

The airport group said the e-mail addresses obtained by the hackers came from passengers signing up to the airports' on-site WiFi.

More detailed data, including vehicle registrations, came from people booking car-park spaces, arranging access to lounges, and booking fast-track.

Customers are urged to remain vigilant about suspicious emails, text messages or phone calls and avoid opening unknown attachments.

Michael Goddard, 71, from Cheshire, said both he and his wife, Julie, 68, had received an email earlier from MAG notifying them that their data had been breached.

"I was shocked," Goddard told BBC Radio Manchester . "To find your personal info has been stolen - it is alarming.

"My information has gone and I don't know what they're going to do with it.

"They have my address in the form of the postcode, they've got my name, so it doesn't take too much to find out who I am.

"I'm not 100% reassured by what Manchester Airports Group has said."

Goddard said he received the email after travelling from East Midlands Airport earlier this year and his wife had used the online booking service for parking at Manchester Airport.

"The concern is there for both of us," he said. "We want the reassurance that if anything happens, they will adequately compensate us."

The identity of the hackers was known, MAG said, and the relevant authorities had been informed.

The Information Commissioner's Office said it was assessing the incident.

"We can confirm we have received a breach report from Manchester Airports Group, and we are assessing the information provided," a spokesperson said.

articles.title: If Meta’s going down, it’s taking TikTok and YouTube with it
articles.summary: Meta’s $17 billion kids online safety settlement with state attorneys general includes an incentive to get rivals on board with design changes for teens.
articles.body: Meta might be on the hook for $17.1 billion and a host of app changes under a new kids safety settlement, but it’s already spinning the deal to its advantage. After years of being the national punching bag for social media harms, Meta has reached a settlement with 47 US states and several districts and territories that gives it a rare opportunity: A chance to flex on its rivals. “We want to ensure teens benefit from this new industry standard, but we cannot do it alone,” Meta says in an “Open Letter” that is also running as a full-page ad in The New York Times, Los Angeles Times, and Washington Post. “These protections will only be truly effective if we work with our peers — TikTok and YouTube — to put the same measures in place.” Snap (which is also named in the agreement), TikTok, and YouTube haven’t yet made a public statement on the settlement and did not respond to requests for comment. By definition, settlements can only constrain the parties that sign them — in this case, Meta and the states. But this deal also names other industry players that both the AGs and Meta would seemingly like to get on board. While Meta will have to pay at least $12 billion to the signing states no matter what (so long as a court approves the deal), the rest of the money is contingent upon changes from three “Core Industry Members”: Snap, TikTok, and YouTube. The multibillion-dollar contingency payment will only be triggered if all three institute some of the same limits Meta’s agreed to for its apps, like daily usage limits and disabling nighttime notifications by default, and the companies that make more than $10 billion in annual profits (TikTok and YouTube) enter settlements with the states for at least as much as Meta’s $5.3 billion contingency payment, “with half of the remaining funds tied to YouTube’s payment and half tied to TikTok’s,” according to Meta. If TikTok and YouTube don’t make the changes and pay up, Meta gets to knock $5 billion off its settlement. (That’s not a lot of money for the company — it reported around $15.8 billion in net revenue last quarter — but it’s not nothing.) If they do, it offsets the disadvantages Meta’s just agreed to and levels the playing field, ensuring teens won’t simply spend their two hours a day on Facebook and Instagram, then flee to YouTube and TikTok. That’s not the only benefit Meta worked in. Another provision notes that its age verification framework will incorporate “reliable age signals shared with Meta by operating systems and app stores operated by Apple and Google.” While this doesn’t diminish Meta’s own obligations, it lays helpful groundwork for Meta as it tries to solidify Apple and Google as key age verification gatekeepers, by ensuring the settlement would be compatible with laws it’s been pushing for across the country. Through this agreement, Meta gets to position itself as the platform that could soon have some of the tightest restrictions for kids in the industry, while trying to cut its rivals down to its new size. And here’s the thing — it might actually work. Meta’s settlement will likely serve as a reference point for all future negotiations around kids online safety. It lays out what one of the biggest industry players not only thinks it can feasibly do, but also what it can live with. It also includes concrete steps for the company to take, rather than a more nebulous standard like the Kids Online Safety Act’s duty of care. It’s conceivable that other platforms will make a similar calculation that these tradeoffs are worth the trouble. If they do, it won’t just be state AGs taking a victory lap, but Meta, too.

articles.title: Australian police arrest two over TeamPCP hacks targeting Mercor, OpenAI, and others | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The arrests come after a wave of cyberattacks earlier this year targeting tech companies that rely on high-profile and widely used open source software.
articles.body:
Australian police have arrested two people in Perth accused of being members of TeamPCP , a prolific hacking group blamed for high-profile hacks against big tech giants in recent months. The two have been charged with more than a dozen hacking, money laundering, and other cybercrime offenses and are expected in court later on Thursday.

According to a statement by the Australian Federal Police, the two men are accused of widespread breaches involving the compromise and tampering of popular open source projects. The hackers aimed to infect a large number of computers to steal credentials and data, then extort victims into paying a ransom.

The FBI’s cyber division chief Brett Leatherman was quoted as saying that the two alleged members of TeamPCP are accused of hacking into more than a thousand organizations as part of their attacks.

It’s unclear whether the Justice Department plans to seek extradition, and a spokesperson for the FBI did not comment when contacted by TechCrunch.

TeamPCP is a prolific cybercriminal gang known for several widespread hacking campaigns targeting the software supply chain, in which the hackers would break in and maliciously modify a popular open source software tool used by potentially thousands of companies.

Once installed on a company’s or developer’s systems, the malicious code steals their private keys and other sensitive credentials used to access cloud storage systems and, oftentimes, customer data. The authorities said the hackers stole more than half a million credentials to further their attacks into other companies.

The hackers were blamed for a cyberattack on the popular vulnerability scanner tool Trivy , which affected any company that relied on it, including LiteLLM , AI recruiting startup Mercor , and others. The hackers are also suspected of breaching the European Commission’s cloud infrastructure , as well as targeting other open source projects and developer apps that allowed access to tech giants like GitHub and OpenAI .

The Australian officials said their investigations began in April 2026 after receiving information from multiple cybersecurity companies.

Police have not named the men who were arrested, but independent cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs exclusively reported that one of the now-arrested alleged hackers is Ruben Thomson, who goes by the hacker handle Ellis. Krebs reported Thursday that he was in contact with Ellis over the past several months, and the hacker told Krebs that he was the leader of TeamPCP until March 2026.

Krebs said Ellis made mistakes that allowed the journalist to learn the alleged hacker’s real identity.

During a press conference on Wednesday announcing the arrests, Australian officials said they had also seized a large quantity of allegedly stolen data, as well as devices and other electronics from the hackers. The officials said they planned to notify victims of the attacks.

articles.title: Trump declares national emergency to ban some foreign grid equipment
articles.summary: President Trump has declared a national emergency seeking to block some foreign equipment from being used in the U.S. electric grid. Trump, in a Wednesday executive order, said foreign supply of electric equipment “constitutes an unusual and extraordinary threat” to national security. He therefore issued the order restricting the purchase and installation of foreign-made components for…
articles.body:
President Trump has declared a national emergency seeking to block some foreign equipment from being used in the U.S. electric grid.

Trump, in a Wednesday executive order , said foreign supply of electric equipment “constitutes an unusual and extraordinary threat” to national security.

He therefore issued the order restricting the purchase and installation of foreign-made components for the grid if doing so poses a risk to grid security or electricity supply.

Under the order, it will be up to Energy Secretary Chris Wright, in coordination with other officials, to determine whether a piece of equipment poses an issue.

The order could impact a wide range of equipment, including substations, transformers, batteries used for energy storage, generators, turbines, software and more.

It does not lay out specific threats or single out any country by name.

However, China is a major manufacturer of a lot of grid equipment , especially solar power and batteries. According to the International Energy Agency , China has 80 percent of the world’s lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity and 85 percent of its solar production capacity.

The Trump administration has called for outpacing China technologically, including on issues such as AI. Separately, it has called for a broader buildout of U.S. energy production, though it has taken a hostile stance toward renewable energy.

Under the last Trump administration, the president put a similar order in place.

The new order comes amid several reported cyberattacks on U.S. water systems, which officials suspect have links to Iran, according to The New York Times .

On his first day in office, Trump declared a national energy emergency as part of an effort to bolster energy production.

articles.title: Americans are cheering for vigilantes who take down Flock cameras
articles.summary: The surveillance cameras have become another flashpoint of growing bipartisan anger against tech industry excess.
articles.body: Americans have declared war on Flock cameras. They’ve protested them, damaged them, and destroyed them. This is only the beginning. The spontaneous and decentralized nature of the vigilante protests is also what makes them difficult to suppress. There isn’t a uniform method of disruption; people have done everything from unplugging, smashing, stealing, and spray-painting the surveillance devices to taking less destructive actions like physically blocking the cameras for hours. Some of the culprits have been caught, but that clearly hasn’t dissuaded others from taking matters into their own hands. Support for those taking drastic measures to get rid of the cameras has also become commonplace online. Last week, a police sheriff in Lumpkin County, Georgia, took to Facebook to announce a $1,000 reward for information leading to the arrest of whoever destroyed a Flock Safety camera installed near a local park. “I hope you’re happy with this. It was to keep our kids safe,” Sheriff Stacy Jarrard said in a video, admonishing the unknown perpetrators while unintentionally confirming what many people already knew: Police are using the cameras to do a lot more than simply give out speeding tickets. The response was not what he was expecting. Jarrard’s post has since received more than 30,000 comments, the vast majority opposing the cameras and many mocking the police and even praising the vandals. “Looks like a Constitutional wind blew it over,” taunted one commenter. “Looks like somebody fixed it for you guys,” wrote another. Others congratulated the culprits, saying those taking direct action to remove the cameras in towns and cities across the US are “doing the lord’s work.” In response to the backlash, Jarrard changed his tone, posting a new video that admitted the need for privacy measures, but stopped short of promising the cameras would be taken down. “We need more safeguards in motion,“ Jarrard said. “I’m going to listen to you.” A few weeks earlier, in suburban New York, police reported a rash of vandalism against Flock cameras in Long Island’s Suffolk County, where four of the cameras had been unplugged, spray-painted, and run over with a car. An article about the incidents in the conservative publication New York Post also attracted a mass of comments opposing the cameras and supporting the people who destroyed them. “They’ve tried to put them up by my house, but someone keeps running them over,” one reader commented on the Post article. “I bet they have gone through a dozen, so far. Thanks to whoever is doing it.” Support for Flock vigilantes has gone beyond internet comments. In one recent case, an Air Force engineer accused of cutting down 13 Flock cameras in Virginia has received over $44,000 for his legal defense from supporters via GoFundMe. In another, felony charges against an alleged Flock vandal in Ohio were dismissed after a grand jury declined to indict the suspect. The fact that so many people seem to not only oppose the cameras but openly support those stealing and destroying them is a historically significant milestone for the anti-Big Tech movement. Activist historians often refer to this approach as a “diversity of tactics” — the idea that movements become stronger when they tolerate those taking extralegal direct action and reject narratives that divide them into “good” and “bad” protesters. As author Margaret Killjoy recently argued in a piece about Flock vandalism: “Social movements are effective specifically when there is solidarity between their broader base and the people who are committing criminal direct action. When social movements stand behind their criminals, they win.” Flock camera destruction isn’t just popular — in some cases, it has also proven highly effective at getting rid of them. Earlier this month, police in Winona, Minnesota, said they would not reinstall the city’s eight Flock cameras after all of them were stolen, citing “growing concerns about trust in policing.” On August 3rd, following two incidents where Flock cameras were destroyed, police in Burnet County, Texas, announced that they had removed all Flock cameras from the area. Like the widespread resistance to AI data centers, support for anti-Flock vigilantism is part of a rapidly growing public sentiment that cuts across geography and political allegiances. The cameras, which have been heavily criticized for their widespread abuse and for being deployed without public hearings or community approval, have quickly become another populist flashpoint of a growing bipartisan movement against tech industry excess. From coastal urban sprawls to rural areas in deep-red states, the message is clear: Folks absolutely despise these things and want them gone by any means necessary. “Nonviolent direct action is a recognized and established tactic, and it’s unsurprising that we are seeing some people are resorting to that,” Alex Marthews, national chair of the nonprofit civil rights group Restore the Fourth, told The Verge. “They’re doing so because the whole structure for approval of surveillance technologies like this has been set up to minimize peoples’ control. Everything gets arranged by public safety people for public safety people, with an explicit intent of shutting the public out. ... What do they expect to happen?” (Flock Safety did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication.) While Flock was initially advertised as an automatic license plate reader system (ALPR), in practice the AI-powered cameras are frequently used by police to track individual vehicles and people based on a wide range of identifying characteristics. In the past month alone, 18 cops in Georgia have been arrested for misusing Flock cameras. A steady stream of media stories has exposed police officers around the country who were stalking their romantic interests, spouses, and other innocent people using the cameras. “People are seeing these cameras in their communities. They are hearing stories of police using them to stalk people. They are reading stories of the tech being used to target immigrants and people exercising their First Amendment rights — and folks are connecting the dots,” Chris Gilliard, an independent privacy researcher and author of the forthcoming book Luxury Surveillance, told The Verge. There still isn’t any scientific data measuring the opposition to Flock nationwide, but smaller polls conducted by research groups and local media outlets show overwhelming opposition to the cameras. According to a recent poll by Spry Research in rural Tennessee’s Knox County, 58 percent of voters say they oppose Flock cameras, and half believe they violate the Fourth Amendment. And in an online poll by NBC News affiliate WJAR in Providence, Rhode Island, 83 percent said they opposed the deployment of Flock cameras in their city or town. Politicians are beginning to catch on, including those from red states. Last month, a trio of House Republicans led by Rep. Tim Burchett (R-TN) introduced a bill to prohibit the federal government from purchasing Flock cameras or similar technology. Republicans in Pennsylvania and West Virginia have put out statements opposing the cameras, with the former urging constituents to call their representatives and tell them to “Stop the Flock.” Legislation that would put warrant restrictions on Flock cameras or ban them outright has been proposed in multiple states, including Maine, Michigan, and Texas. And a man who was running for a seat in the Tennessee House of Representatives was recently arrested after allegedly shooting four different cameras with a gun. Marthews says the bipartisan opposition to Flock across the country confounds the idea that privacy and civil rights are the exclusive purview of left-leaning communities. “The MAGA base does not like this stuff. They do not like being intruded upon in matters intrinsic to their everyday life,” Marthews told The Verge. “If you’re talking about rural areas, you’re going to be driving everywhere. They don’t have a choice about whether to drive, and therefore they don’t have a choice about whether Flock is sucking up all this information about everywhere they go.” Dozens of cities and counties across the US have now terminated, rejected, or declined to renew contracts with Flock Safety since the beginning of last year. In total, more than 130 cities have rejected ALPR systems, according to the site DeFlock, which maintains a map revealing the locations of Flock cameras across the country. Opposition to the technology is even impacting the real estate market — some homebuyers are using the DeFlock map to avoid buying property in areas where the cameras have been deployed. Even Flock CEO Garrett Langley has been forced to soften his stance toward anti-Flock activists. He recently apologized for comments in a previous interview where he referred to DeFlock as a “terroristic” group. He has also announced changes to the software. Viet Trinh, a historian and professor of ethnic studies at Ohio State University who testified against Flock cameras in a recent hearing, says the public and performative nature of Flock vandalism is another aspect of its viral popularity. “It’s not just that they see the camera and take it down. Even when the people who destroy these cameras are caught, there’s a public intrigue to it,” Trinh told The Verge. “The fact that nobody likes these cameras and that there’s someone out there willing to do something about it captures the public imagination.” Gilliard doesn’t think it’s a coincidence that the vigilante actions against Flock cameras are occurring simultaneously with widespread protests against power-hungry data centers. In a sense, they are simply the most convenient and visible targets of a growing populist anger against Silicon Valley and its ongoing obsession with forcing AI and surveillance into every aspect of our lives. “It’s easier to deface a camera than it would be to smash Claude or ChatGPT,” said Gilliard. Despite the recent momentum, advocates like Marthews worry that too much of the pushback is limited to Flock itself. Even now, competitors like Axon smell blood in the water, and they’re moving in to capitalize on the widespread public scrutiny of the company. It highlights what privacy advocates see as a critical vulnerability in the current tech backlash movement — the tendency to focus on one or two highly villainized companies instead of the technologies and systems themselves. “A lot of this seems like anti-Flock rather than anti-surveillance,” said Gilliard. “Unfortunately as with most things, people often don’t feel moved unless a thing affects them personally. I think it’s an important moment because reformers are talking more and more about ‘guardrails,’ when the proper solution is abolition.” Whatever form the pushback might take in the future, Flock has made clear that the popular anger against the tech industry isn’t confined to one political party — and those taking action aren’t being constrained by what is legal. “There is this visceral understanding that this technology is a surveillance tech that more or less criminalizes anyone who drives a car or sits in a car,” said Trinh. “People who are on the right and normally support these punitive measures imagine that they don’t apply to them. But I think what’s happening with this tech is there’s now a very intuitive understanding that in this case, everyone is a criminal.”

articles.title: Analysis-Bessent, Warsh diverge on who should set the price of money
articles.summary: By Karen Brettell Aug 27 (Reuters) - Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh appear at odds over a question at the heart of...
articles.body:
Aug 27 (Reuters) - Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh appear at odds over a question at the heart of U.S. financial policy. How hands-off can policymakers be when it comes to setting a price for money?

Warsh has advocated retreating from some of the central bank's longstanding ‌communication policies in favor of letting markets do the heavy lifting, while Bessent has deployed a number of tools, some of them unusual, in the name of ‌aiding market function.

The divide has come into view as the Trump administration steps up efforts to contain long-term borrowing costs — a push whose success appears unlikely to many analysts and portfolio managers without concrete steps to contain the sprawling ​U.S. fiscal deficit.

That contrast in approaches will come into focus on Friday morning, when Warsh is scheduled to speak at the Fed's annual event in Jackson Hole, Wyoming. He wants bond markets to play a bigger role in setting rates, a stance arguably at odds with Bessent's interventionism. Meanwhile investors are seeking assurance that Warsh will act decisively against inflation in his first year leading a divided Fed.

Bessent said last week Treasury would at least double buybacks of longer-dated debt, arguing that a rise in yields, which pushed 30-year rates to a 19-year high, didn't reflect ‌fundamentals. Investors read it as a sign Washington won't let 10-year ⁠yields, which drive mortgage rates, approach 5% unanswered.

Many investors say Bessent is fighting the wrong fight. They say strong growth, sticky inflation, likely Fed hikes and heavy bond supply, including from AI-driven corporate borrowing, are what's pushing yields up, along with a widening fiscal premium tied to the deficit — ⁠not market dysfunction.

Billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller, a hedge-fund titan and workplace mentor to both men, called the plan "price management" rather than liquidity management and warned it could damage Treasury's credibility.

"There's very little evidence that Treasuries are oversold right now," said Will Compernolle, macro strategist at FHN Financial.

Traders say that pressure will surface elsewhere if bond yields aren't allowed to rise to a market-clearing price — including in a dollar that ​has ​slid since Bessent's announcement.

Bessent's strategy appears aimed at easing the economy's interest burden ​while preserving growth. He says Treasury has a large toolkit, but its ‌influence over long-term yields is constrained by cash management, financing needs and that the U.S. will follow a predictable issuance schedule.

articles.title: Trump Renames Lake Ontario as Lake America, Stoking Canada Spat
articles.summary: President Donald Trump announced he was moving to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, escalating his clash with Canada after trade negotiations between the...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump announced he was moving to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, escalating his clash with Canada after trade negotiations between the two nations collapsed.

Trump on Thursday signed a directive changing the name of the lake and said the move would take place "effective immediately." The president previewed the move in a social media post earlier this week.

"Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade," Trump told reporters when asked what message he was sending to the US's northern neighbor. "They want to be treated like they're a state, and so we just can't do that anymore."

Lake Ontario is one of the Great Lakes and straddles the US-Canada border between the state of New York and the province of Ontario. Canada is virtually certain to reject Trump's unilateral move to rename the body of water.

Trump last year renamed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America, another jab at a US neighbor and major trading partner.

articles.title: ATF declares ‘major incident’ as ransomware gang claims hack
articles.summary: The ATF is the latest federal government agency in recent years to notify Congress of a "major incident" involving its cybersecurity.
articles.body:
The U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, or ATF, says a cyberattack on one of its systems has been declared a “major incident,” a formal, legally defined classification that prompts a formal notification to lawmakers in Congress.

ATF said in a statement that it’s responding to the cyberattack on a stand-alone system that’s separate from the bureau’s network. An ATF spokesperson told reporters that the targeted computer system contained information such as the “targets of ATF investigations.”

TechCrunch has seen a claim of responsibility by the Qilin ransomware gang on its leak site, but it did not provide evidence for its claim, such as a sample of leaked data. Qilin is known for running a “ransomware-as-a-service” operation, in which it leases its hacking tools to other criminal affiliates for a cut of the profits. The gang has listed media giant Lee Enterprises and U.K. pathology lab giant Synnovis as targets.

Under federal law, “major incidents” include significant cyber incidents that are likely to cause demonstrable harm to U.S. national security or broader U.S. interests. Agencies are requi r ed to disclose major incidents to Congress within a week of their discovery.

The ATF joins several government agencies in recent years that have declared major incidents following a breach, including a 2023 ransomware attack on a system used by the U.S. Marshals Service , and a breach of an FBI system earlier this year that exposed phone numbers of targets under surveillance by federal agents.

articles.title: As Jackson Hole conference kicks off, three Fed officials issue inflation warnings
articles.body:
Aug 27 (Reuters) - Federal Reserve officials shared on Thursday their ongoing concerns about the U.S. inflation landscape, as central bankers gathered in Jackson Hole, Wyoming for the Kansas City Fed's closely watched annual economic symposium.

Inflation is "still stubborn and it's still sticky and we've got to continue to find ways to break through" and get it back to 2%, Kansas City Fed President ‌Jeffrey Schmid said on CNBC on the sidelines of the conference.

He noted that the U.S. central bank's current policy rate, which was left in the 3.50%-3.75% range at the July 28-29 meeting, did not appear ‌to be restrictive. "I don't know what we're restricting currently with the rate policy that we're at today," Schmid said.

Schmid, who had recently been in favor of raising rates to help bring inflation back down to the Fed's 2% target, seemed to suggest that he would still favor such ​a path, given his belief that monetary policy is not working to counter current price pressures.

But even so, when asked about the outlook for a rate hike at the Fed's September 15-16 policy meeting, he said, "I think we need a little bit more information. What I'm trying to figure out is the demand side of what's driving both growth and inflation."

Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, also speaking on CNBC, was similarly anxious about inflation and reiterated her ongoing willingness to act to bring price pressures back in line.

"I don't want to prejudge anything," Hammack said, "but I believe now is the time to act."

Hammack, one of three Fed officials who dissented at last month's meeting in favor of a rate hike, said inflation has been above ‌target for more than five years and monetary policy is not doing anything at ⁠the moment to restrain the economy in order to lower price pressures.

The Cleveland Fed chief said she is hearing more and more from contacts worried about inflation and she fears the longer this trend continues, the greater the risk to the central bank's credibility. Information from local contacts suggests "we're starting to get some of that inflationary mindset" embedding itself in the ⁠economy. "I don't think we're there yet, but that's what I want to make sure we avoid," Hammack said.

In a later interview on the Fox Business Network, Hammack said she believes the job market is in balance and that the U.S. central bank appears unlikely to achieve its price pressure target even by next year. "My forecast is that inflation is going to end this year around 3% and I think we're not going to make significant progress next year. I think we'll get to maybe mid-twos at best," Hammack ​said ​on the network's "Big Money Show" program.

articles.title: Relief at VW Chemnitz plant amid fears carmaker plans drastic cuts
articles.summary: As VW board members tour sites throughout Germany holding crisis talks with staff, state lawmakers expressed frustration about the outlook on Thursday. "It i...
articles.body:
As VW board members tour sites throughout Germany holding crisis talks with staff, state lawmakers expressed frustration about the outlook on Thursday.

"It is my clear expectation of the Executive Board that they will ensure a viable plan for the future," Lower Saxony's premier Olaf Lies told dpa. "Plant closures and mass redundancies cannot be the solution."

His comments come after VW boss Oliver Blume said he plans to expand cost-cutting measures, triggering fears at Europe's largest carmaker that tens of thousands of additional jobs and four entire sites could be at risk.

Blume's comments led to anger at the powerful works council, and a slew of extraordinary staff meetings at nine sites.

VW's management board began a tour of its sites on Tuesday. After visits to the plants in Emden and Zwickau - considered to be at risk - the board representatives headwed for the engine plant in Chemnitz and a plant in Dresden. However, the Dresden talks were called off as no urgent talks were needed there, works council spokesman Heiko Lossie said.

VW has not been producing cars in Dresden since the end of last year. After 24 years of series production, the last car rolled off the production line in December and now, an innovation campus is being developed together with Dresden University of Technology and 230 workers are to keep their jobs for the time being.

The staff meeting with VW board member Thomas Schmall gave a positive signal to the Chemnitz engine plant. Financial figures, production figures and capacity use in Chemnitz are excellent, and the order books are full, said Christian Sommer, VW Saxony spokesman said after the meeting.

Works council chairman Olaf Glöckner also described the mood following Schmall's visit as positive.

Beyond Emden and Zwickau, there are no viable plans for the commercial vehicle plant in Hanover and the Audi site in Neckarsulm for the 2030s.

"However, I would also like to make it clear that no decision has been made regarding possible plant closures," said Blume. The aim is to create robust prospects for all sites over the next six to twelve months.

He has recently underlined that the problems facing the carmaker are not internal VW problems. "The entire car industry is under enormous pressure," he said, pointing to US tariffs, market developments in China and several political crises as factors affecting all major manufacturers and suppliers alike.

Industry observer Stefan Bratzel from the Centre of Automotive Management said Volkswagen must achieve a "quantum leap" as it looks to the future.

articles.title: Why August is the most dangerous month to ignore your data
articles.summary: Medicare Open Enrollment scams start with data broker targeting months before October. Learn why August is the time to remove your personal info.
articles.body: Medicare Open Enrollment doesn't start until Oct. 15. So why am I telling you to worry about this in August? Because by the time October 15 arrives, scammers aren't starting their work. They're finishing it. The scam calls you may hear this fall, including fake Medicare card offers and urgent Social Security warnings, are only the final step. Scammers often build their target lists long before they make contact. Here is how that targeting process works and what you can do now to make yourself and your family harder to scam. THIS SATURDAY! Free live CyberGuy class: Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward. Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com. DR OZ WARNS MEDICARE SCAMMERS ARE STEALING BILLIONS — AND YOUR PERSONAL INFORMATION COULD BE NEXT The dates that shape fall benefit scams Two major dates put Medicare and Social Security on the minds of millions of Americans each fall. Oct. 15 Medicare Open Enrollment begins on October 15 and runs through December 7. During that period, people can review their coverage and make certain changes that generally take effect Jan. 1. That also means beneficiaries expect to receive plan information, advertisements and calls about their coverage. Oct. 14, 2026 The Bureau of Labor Statistics currently plans to release September 2026 inflation data on Oct. 14. That release will complete the third-quarter CPI-W figures used to calculate the 2027 Social Security COLA. The Social Security Administration says the next COLA will be announced in October 2026. Based on the current schedule, the announcement is expected on October 14. The Senior Citizens League currently projects a 3.8% increase for 2027. That estimate has been generating headlines, but it isn't the official number. The final percentage will depend on inflation data for July, August and September. Scammers do not have to guess when people will be thinking about benefits. These dates are public and repeat every year. The part that happens before the phone rings Here's what almost nobody thinks about. A scam call often comes near the end of the process, not the beginning. Before a fraudster dials, someone has to decide whom to target. Consumer lists can help make that decision. The Justice Department has already shown in court how marketing data can end up in the hands of scammers. How Epsilon helped fraudsters find targets Epsilon Data Management maintained a database covering roughly 100 million American households. Two former employees, Robert Reger and David Lytle, spent about a decade selling targeted consumer lists to people running fraud schemes. Epsilon used consumer data and algorithms to identify people who were likely to respond to certain offers. One fraudster bought nearly 100 lists and used them to defraud more than 218,000 victims of over $23.7 million. Epsilon paid $150 million to resolve the case. That included $22.5 million in criminal penalties and $127.5 million for victim compensation. In September 2024, a federal court sentenced Reger to 120 months in prison and Lytle to 48 months. Other marketing companies supplied fraud operations Epsilon was not alone. KBM Group employees sold consumer data to clients involved in fraudulent mass-mailing schemes. The company entered into an agreement requiring it to pay $33.5 million for victim compensation and an $8.5 million criminal fine. Macromark pleaded guilty to knowingly supplying lists of potential victims to fraudulent mass mailers. Many of the victims were older and vulnerable. The company agreed to pay $1 million in fines and forfeiture. These companies did not operate from hidden corners of the dark web. They were established marketing businesses with employees, clients and offices. Targeted lists remain easy to buy Legitimate marketing companies still sell consumer lists online. Vendors advertise databases of Americans age 65 and older, along with lists created specifically for businesses that want to contact people approaching their 65th birthday. Buyers can often filter those lists by age, location, income, homeownership and other demographic details. Some products also include names, mailing addresses, phone numbers, email addresses and estimated home values. Selling a marketing list does not automatically make the vendor or buyer a scammer. However, the market shows how easily someone can identify and contact a narrow group of older Americans. That is why August and September matter. The personal data already exists, the enrollment dates are public and anyone planning a fall fraud campaign can begin researching potential targets before the calls start. WHAT A SCAMMER SEES THE MOMENT THEY GOOGLE YOUR NAME Where your data broker profile comes in A purchased list gets a scammer a name, an age, and an address. That alone makes for a generic call. What turns a generic call into a convincing one is everything else that's sitting on people-search sites like Spokeo, Whitepages, BeenVerified and Intelius. As I've written before, those profiles routinely include address history, relatives' names, and financial signals like property ownership and estimated home value. That's the difference between "Hello, I'm calling about your Medicare benefits" and "Hi Mr. Patterson, I'm calling about the plan at your address on Maple Street. Is your wife Linda still on the same coverage?" One of those calls gets hung up on. The other one gets answered. You can run a quick free scan of how exposed you are online to get a better understanding of your data exposure. If it shows details you never consented to publishing, you'll be able to take action and get them removed. Get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web: CyberGuy.com. What the numbers actually show A data removal service research team analyzed FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center data and found that 72% of the crimes reported by Americans over 60 in 2024 were facilitated or made worse by victims' personal data being available online. That's roughly 82,000 complaints out of 113,906. Those data-facilitated crimes accounted for $4.2 billion of the $4.9 billion older Americans reported losing that year. The average victim lost about $33,200. And this problem is growing, not shrinking. Reported elder fraud victims rose 45% in a single year. What the fall adds isn't a new kind of crime. It's a schedule. The Federal Trade Commission puts it plainly: "Every year, scammers get more active around Medicare Open Enrollment Period, trying to get your money, information, or both." The agency warns that callers pose as Medicare representatives, pressure people about a "new" or "updated" Medicare card, and spoof caller ID so the call appears to come from an official number. Meanwhile, the Social Security version writes itself. Every October, a wave of "Claim Your COLA" scams tells retirees they have to take action to receive their increase or they'll lose it. They don't. The adjustment is automatic. But by October, that call arrives sounding perfectly timed, because it is. 'I'll worry about this when the calls actually start' That's the natural reaction. October feels like the real deadline. Why act now? Because the targeting gets locked in before the calls do. If your name, age, address, relatives, and financial profile are sitting on broker sites this month, they're available to be compiled, sorted, and resold well before anyone picks up a phone in October. And removal isn't instant. Brokers have to process opt-out requests, and they re-list information on a rolling basis, which means the process works best when you start it early and let it run. Beginning in August means you're being scrubbed from the pipeline while it's still being assembled. Beginning in November means you're filing paperwork while the calls are already coming in. The point isn't to react faster. It's to be a worse target before anyone goes looking. How to get ahead of the cycle now These steps can help reduce the personal information scammers may use and prepare your family before fall fraud attempts begin. 1) Search for yourself first Go to Spokeo, Whitepages, BeenVerified or a similar site and look up your own name. See exactly what a caller would see this month, before they do. 2) Do it for your parents too If you have older relatives, their profiles are the ones worth the most to a scammer. An August check-in beats an October warning. WHY CAREFUL PEOPLE STILL END UP ON DATA BROKER SITES 3) Submit opt-out requests now, not in October Every major broker is required to honor removal requests. The catch: there are hundreds of them, each with its own process, and they re-list your information regularly. Starting now gives the process time to work before the fall surge. 4) Use an automated data removal service Removing your information from data brokers one site at a time can take hours. A reputable automated data removal service can submit opt-out requests on your behalf and continue checking participating sites in case your information reappears. Some services also accept custom removal requests for people-search sites and other websites that publish personal details. Before signing up, compare the number of brokers covered, how often the service checks for new listings, whether it handles custom requests and whether independent experts have reviewed its privacy and security practices. A family plan may offer better value when you want to protect parents, children or other members of your household. No service can remove every piece of information from the internet, but ongoing removals can reduce the personal details scammers may use to create convincing calls, messages or emails. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com. 5) Set a family password now, before the calls start Agree on a code word with elderly parents or relatives today, while there's no pressure. It's a much easier conversation in August than in the middle of a panicked phone call in November. 6) Change your security questions If your bank still verifies you with "mother's maiden name" or "city you were born in," that information is likely already on a broker profile. Switch to answers that aren't true and store them in a password manager. Kurt's key takeaways Medicare Open Enrollment runs from October 15 through December 7, while the 2027 Social Security COLA is expected to be announced on October 14. Those public dates give scammers predictable events to reference in calls, texts and letters. Justice Department cases involving Epsilon, KBM Group and Macromark show that consumer information has been sold to fraud operations and used to identify older or vulnerable targets. The FBI received 201,266 complaints from people 60 and older in 2025, with reported losses reaching $7.748 billion. Incogni separately estimated that exposed personal information may have facilitated or worsened 72% of the 2024 crime categories it analyzed. Removing information from people-search sites cannot prevent every scam. However, reducing exposed details can make it harder for a criminal to create a convincing personal story. Social Security COLA increases are automatic. Medicare cards are mailed automatically and are free. Anyone demanding information or payment to activate either one should be treated as a potential scammer. You still have time before this year's open enrollment period begins. Search your name today and see what a stranger can learn before ever picking up the phone. Has a scammer ever used personal details to make a Medicare or Social Security call seem legitimate? articles.title: Major tech companies call for defensive surge to defeat AI-driven hacks
articles.summary: Major tech companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon are calling for a society-wide defensive surge to defeat what they describe as an impending wave of hacks driven by artificial intelligence.
articles.body: Major tech companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon are calling for a society-wide defensive surge to defeat what they describe as an impending wave of hacks driven by artificial intelligence. In a joint letter issued Thursday, the companies — along with more than 100 others including Broadcom, Capital One, Cloudflare, CrowdStrike, General Motors, IBM, Mastercard, Oracle, Robinhood, Shopify and Visa — said there was a limited amount of time “to make our digital world much more secure” ahead of the AI threat. “In the coming months, AI-enabled cyberattacks will become far more widespread as models around the world become increasingly capable,” the letter said. It called on government and industry leaders “to bring the full weight of their technology, resources, and expertise to this effort.” It called on governments to expedite trusted access programs, which give certain companies access to more powerful models ahead of the general public, and for all other organizations to “make cyber defense an immediate leadership priority.” The U.S. cyberdefense agency CISA and the White House did not immediately return a message seeking comment. President Donald Trump’s administration imposed deep cuts on CISA when it took office and the agency’s staffing fell by about a third last year. Meanwhile fears that advances in AI will supercharge hacking campaigns are being realized as rogue elements increasingly deploy large language models to break into organizations around the world. In June, the world’s “Five Eyes” intelligence alliance — composed of the U.S., Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand — issued a rare joint statement warning that the AI revolution was poised to “fundamentally transform” cybersecurity.
